summary: A global fintech running OpenClaw agents in Security, Finance, Compliance, HR, Engineering and Anti-Fraud details its secrets architecture: credentials live in 1Password, every retrieval requires a biometric TouchID approval via the desktop app, and a tmux session isolates secrets in memory only during a workflow.

title: How I Rebuilt My AI Agent Team After the Lobster Lobotomy

title: Agent minimalism: what shipping OpenClaw in production taught us
summary: AutoClaw, an OpenClaw deployment consultancy, measured a 650× token overhead (~20,000 tokens for a trivial "hello" vs 30 tokens via plain API) from OpenClaw's injected context (system prompt ~7k, workspace files ~3k, tool registry ~1k, schemas ~3.4k, all re-sent on every call). They walked away from OpenClaw for two production cases — an SRE agent on Cloudflare Workers and data-discovery chatbots — replacing them with deterministic pipelines plus one tight LLM call. Includes a decision rule for when to reach for an agent framework vs plain code, and an open-source deployment playbook.

title: credence-pi — Bayesian model routing, waste blocking, and injection detection for OpenClaw
summary: An OpenClaw plugin + local daemon that holds one Bayesian belief about your agent, learned from your own approvals and refusals: routes each tool call to the cheapest sufficient model (trying cheap first, escalating only when payoff covers it), blocks exact-repeat tool calls, and surfaces prompt-injected actions for confirmation before they fire. Includes shadow mode for auditing before enforcing. Real benchmarks on 17 Terminal-Bench tasks show it beats every fixed single-model choice for every user type.

title: OpenEmployee — deny-by-default governance, budgets, and audit trails for OpenClaw agents

Demos: a finance PA that blocks a $1,500 IRS bill exceeding a $1,000/mo budget, an SDR that blocks a poisoned lead redirecting to all-staff@, and DLP catching an API key in an email body — all enforced deterministically, no model in the loop.

Supports US + Canada numbers, prompt-to-call setup ("call +1234567890"), and works with Claude Code, Cursor, Hermes, and OpenClaw.

title: Outpost — capability-based credential proxy for AI agents
summary: A reverse proxy that gives OpenClaw (and other AI agents) capabilities instead of credentials: agents never see raw API keys. Outpost injects auth, enforces rate limits, path allow/deny lists, sensitive-write gates, and source-IP allowlists. Deployable to Cloudflare Workers (free tier) or Docker. 10 built-in auth modules, 3-line provider YAMLs, and a comparison table against MITM alternatives.

Honest about OpenClaw's 100k-200k token-per-message context bloat.

title: Pinch: Autonomous AI Content Engine That Drafts But Never Posts Without Approval
summary: Pinch is an always-on content agent built on OpenClaw that monitors release feeds, identifies updates worth writing about, and drafts platform-specific content (X threads, LinkedIn posts, YouTube descriptions) in the author's voice via a SOUL.md personality contract. All drafts are delivered via Telegram for one-word human approval (approve, tweak, or skip) before any manual publishing. The builder conducted explicit prompt-injection adversarial testing before going live, feeding fake release notes with hidden injection payloads to verify the agent correctly flagged and stopped on manipulated input. Security architecture: fetched content goes into structured fields, flagged inputs stop execution, scanning layer has zero publishing permissions. Open-sourced on GitHub.

title: Anicca: Autonomous Self-Healing Agent Patched 79 Broken Cron Jobs
summary: Anicca is an autonomous AI agent running on a Mac Mini via OpenClaw cron jobs with the mission to 'keep myself alive: post content, reply to mail, fix my own bugs, earn money for the GPU bill.' This post documents a real incident: 79 of 100+ cron jobs broke with 'Invalid request body.' The agent shipped three fixes: a Universal Observer polling Gmail, Postiz, and the OpenClaw cron registry every 30 minutes; a Reflexion-meets-Voyager self-fixing layer that auto-scaffolds learned skills when the same symptom hits >=3 times in 30 days; and a critical security bug caught in its own code generation — a heredoc that expanded shell metacharacters from LLM output. Split into literal data file + wrapper script. Honest about not having earned back the GPU bill yet.

title: Betty LD: Self-Hosted Instagram Agent for Car Market Analytics
summary: A real deployed agentic workflow on a self-hosted Ubuntu node with Dockerized OpenClaw that scrapes second-hand car auction listings, evaluates fair prices based on preservation, maintenance, and condition, and drafts Instagram posts with generated images via a self-hosted Postiz instance. Uses TECHNIQUES.md as long-term workflow memory, skills in /app/skills, tmux transparency, and Telegram notifications. Honest about model deprecation forcing two migrations in three months and the 'N pattern' of agentic development.

title: Kelviq Business Vetting: Automating Merchant-of-Record Verification with OpenClaw
summary: Co-founder of Kelviq (an MoR platform) built an automated business verification system on OpenClaw over a weekend. Profile submission triggers a Discord message; the agent analyzes the website, compares it against policies, and outputs an approval or rejection with detailed reasoning, category, and confidence score. Stack: OpenClaw on DigitalOcean + OpenRouter + Discord. Solves a real operational pain: surge in verification requests causing constant context switching and drain.

title: I Built a 23-Agent AI System That Runs My Real Businesses. Here's What Nobody Tells You.
summary: Twenty-three OpenClaw agents across a Mac Mini and Ubuntu VPS managing five real businesses (two ISPs, outdoor media, holdings, AI agency). Brutally honest confession: while one agent (Felix) made $177K for someone else, the entire constellation made only $17. Three disasters: (1) CTO agent Elon set compaction.mode to 'auto' -- silently invalid, degraded API times from 40ms to 12 seconds; (2) a Unicode zero-width space (U+200B) hidden in a JSON key caused 3-day group-resolution failure; (3) eight orphan processes polling the same Telegram token created a 409 Conflict feedback loop the ops agent made worse by spawning diagnostics. Every failure becomes a same-day HEARTBEAT.md rule. Core insight: agents don't fail because of bad code -- they fail because nobody holds them to a number.

title: Multi-Agent Research Pipeline: 4× Faster, ~$0.16/Article with OpenClaw Concurrent Sub-Agents
summary: A production research pipeline using four specialized OpenClaw agents (Scout, Analyst, Verifier, Writer) running concurrently via sub-agent spawning. Real metrics over 8 articles: 2-3 hours -> 25-40 minutes per article (4× faster), 8-12 sources consulted vs 4-6 manually (2× coverage), 80% fewer factual errors thanks to a dedicated Verifier agent. Cost: ~$0.16/article by routing search/verify to DeepSeek V4 Flash and analysis/writing to Claude Sonnet 4.6. Key insight: concurrent sub-agents provide the speedup, not the model; structured JSON handoffs between agents prevent the biggest early failure mode; cron scheduling enables overnight processing with a structured brief ready by morning.

title: I Ran an AI Agent for 30 Days Straight -- Here's the Boring Engineering That Made It Work
summary: One OpenClaw agent running every 6 hours for 30 days processing real customer support emails: classification, draft replies, thread tagging. 120 scheduled runs, 117 successful completions, 14 dead-letter items out of ~6,000 (0.23%), only 3 human interventions total. Four critical fixes: queue+checkpointing after OOM crash (day 4), exponential backoff after infinite retry burned $40 (day 9), persistent Postgres state after restart caused stale replies (day 14), infrastructure tax handing off to non-technical operators (day 19). Core lesson: agents fail because nobody wires up the boring stuff.

title: OpenClaw Factory: 33 autonomous Claude agents, 6 months of production
summary: Six months running a multi-agent Claude system across four businesses using 33 sharply-scoped agents with narrow charters and persistent memory. ~$2.4K/month Claude spend, buying back ~44 founder hours/week. Real metrics: 4.1% reversal rate, 11% re-prompt rate, median 2.3K tokens reference memory per agent. Key insight: charter narrowness beats agent intelligence. Inter-agent communication uses stripped JSON envelopes (not prose), cutting token spend ~40%. Planner drift caught with hard checkpoints every 10 turns. Opus reserved for planning; Sonnet on inner loop. Honest about failures and lessons.

title: OpenClaw: 13 Errors, $1.50/Month, and an AI Team That Doesn't Need the Cloud
summary: A team of AI agents running on a 2022 Mac with a local 30-billion-parameter model in Docker. Zero API fees, zero cloud provider. Agents handle Slack triage (summarizing threads, flagging action items), multi-source research with parallel sub-agents, content drafting, and infrastructure monitoring. Performance tuned from 12 tokens/sec to 49. Full cost breakdown: $1.50/month electricity vs. $330/month previously paid for cloud APIs. Honest about every config that matters and all 13 errors hit along the way.

title: I Ran OpenClaw and Claude Side by Side for 3 Months
summary: A real production comparison: Claude is a chat interface; OpenClaw is a personal agent that acts. Morning inbox clearing, calendar conflict checks, and follow-up reminders ran in the background while the user had coffee. Persistent memory across sessions was the bigger deal than expected -- tone preferences, ongoing projects, and timezone carry over automatically. Honest about the 45-minute setup vs Claude's 30-second onboarding.

title: OpenClaw's $1.3 Million OpenAI Bill: What AI Agents Actually Cost in Production
summary: Peter Steinberger's first public cost breakdown: 100 agents consumed 603 billion tokens and 7.6 million API requests in one month, totalling $1,305,088.81. Agents reviewed PRs, scanned commits, deduplicated issues, wrote fixes, monitored benchmarks, and attended meetings. Disabling Fast Mode would drop the bill to ~$300K/month ($3,000/agent). OpenAI covers it as a research investment -- regular companies don't get that deal.

title: My AI Agent Kept Making Shit Up (And Other Lessons From Running OpenClaw)
summary: Six-week production postmortem running DeepSeek V3 in Docker: hallucinations, silent config failures, broken tool schemas, exec approval mazes, and the realization that LLMs can be compulsive liars in certain contexts. Agent named Sabrina pulled RSS feeds and Reddit, synthesized news, and emailed daily briefs. Honest about what worked (multi-model, email delivery, Docker isolation) and what didn't (Slack integration ripped out, report engine over-promised).
